/**
 * Prose rules (r3-fixes 2.9, D6): the RULES above minus the two that read a
 * command line's grammar into ordinary words. A flag must start a word here
 * (`re-authenticate [redacted] user` is not `-authenticate [redacted] and a header
 * needs its scheme (`Authorization:  [redacted] need sign-off` is a sentence). Private
 * key blocks are added: a prompt is where one gets pasted whole.
 */
const PROSE_RULES: Array<{ re: RegExp; replace: string }> = [
  RULES[0]!,
  { re: new RegExp(`(^|\\s)(--?${SECRET_NAME})(=|[ \\t]+)${VALUE}`, 'gi'), replace: `$1$2$3${REDACTED}` },
  { re: /\b((?:proxy-)?authorization\s*:\s*)(bearer|basic|token|digest)\s+(?:"[^"]*"|'[^']*'|\S+)/gi, replace: `$1$2 ${REDACTED}` },
  RULES[3]!,
  RULES[4]!,
  { re: /-----BEGIN [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----[\s\S]*?-----END [A-Z ]*PRIVATE KEY-----/g, replace: REDACTED },
]

/**
 * Redact credential-shaped material from the operator's prose before it
 * enters the committed record — the deterministic scrub a kept prompt passes
 * (r3-fixes 2.9, D6). Same bias as redactCommand: a `[redacted]` in a brief
 * costs less than a live credential in an append-only, replicated log.
 */
export function redactProse(text: string): string {
  let out = text
  for (const { re, replace } of PROSE_RULES) out = out.replace(re, replace)
  return out
}
EOF

payload.chose: 2.6 supersede-target integrity, in three parts. (1) Two-key hold. A decision can name a target its own words barely match (TF-IDF cosine under 0.16) while an in-force decision it could retire matches at least 2.5 times as much and at least 0.16. Or it can name a target that is already replaced or retired. Then the writer files it with the link held: supersedes moves to supersedes_held, link_candidates holds the named target first, then up to 2 better matches (or its replacement). The target stays in force. The write result, the digest and Stop ask for `sofar supersedes`. SOFAR_LINK_HOLD=off is the ablation arm. (2) decisions.md prints each entry's handle with a check suffix, D17·k3fz (4 Crockford base32 chars of sha256 of the event id). Every write path accepts D17·k3fz. When a merge moved the ordinal, it resolves by the suffix; it refuses a suffix that names nothing. The digest keeps bare [D<n>]. (3) Write results echo what a supersession retired, or that it retired nothing.

Refusing low-relatedness links: a refusal costs a resend, and a flagged link may be right.  * Two-key supersession (r3-fixes 2.6, D18). A named target is suspect when it
 * shares less than this with the new decision's words (TF-IDF cosine)...
 */
export const HOLD_NAMED_MAX = 0.16
/** ...and another in-force decision it could retire shares at least this many times as much, and at least HOLD_NAMED_MAX. */
export const HOLD_RATIO = 2.5

/** `SOFAR_LINK_HOLD=off` (the ablation arm): a named target is taken as named, as before 2.6. */
export function linkHoldEnabled(env: Record<string, string | undefined> = process.env): boolean {
  return env.SOFAR_LINK_HOLD !== 'off'
}

type Draft = { chose: string; over: string; because: string; rule?: string }

/**
 * The second key of a supersession (r3-fixes 2.6, D18): null when the link
 * the writer was given stands; otherwise it is HELD, and this is what to
 * offer instead, best first, at most LINK_CANDIDATES_MAX - 1 (maybe none).
 *
 * Round 3 retired the wrong entry twice in 3 reps: a Cursor session named a
 * guarded rule beside the one it changed, and a Claude session named a
 * D-number counted from a raw events.jsonl read, whose file order a merge had
 * moved. Both named a target their words barely touched (cosine 0.129 and 0
 * here) while an in-force decision matched 2.5× and more. A handle is one
 * key; what the decision's own words match is a second, independent one. When
 * they disagree this far the link is held, never refused: the decision is
 * filed, the target stays in force, and the agent confirms one or the other.
 * A target already replaced (the fold would silently re-point it) or no
 * longer in force is held the same way, offering its live replacement — the
 * refusal `sofar supersedes` gives for the same answer. Writer-side only: the
 * verdict is stamped into the payload, so no reader recomputes it.
 */
export function linkHold(state: InitiativeState, draft: Draft, target: number): number[] | null {
  const named = state.decisions[target - 1]
  if (named === undefined) return null
  // A plain decision naming a rule retires nothing (D25): nothing to protect.
  if (named.rule !== undefined && draft.rule === undefined) return null
  const retirable = (n: number): boolean => state.decisions[n - 1]!.rule === undefined || draft.rule !== undefined
  if (named.superseded_by !== undefined) {
    let head = named.superseded_by
    while (state.decisions[head - 1]?.superseded_by !== undefined) head = state.decisions[head - 1]!.superseded_by!
    return retirable(head) && !retiredOrdinals(state).has(head) ? [head] : []
  }
  const retired = retiredOrdinals(state)
  if (retired.has(target)) return []
  const scores = relatedness(state, draft)
  const score = scores[target - 1]!
  if (score >= HOLD_NAMED_MAX) return null
  const bar = Math.max(HOLD_RATIO * score, HOLD_NAMED_MAX)
  const better: Array<{ ordinal: number; score: number }> = []
  state.decisions.forEach((d, i) => {
    const ordinal = i + 1
    if (ordinal === target || d.superseded_by !== undefined || retired.has(ordinal) || !retirable(ordinal)) return
    if (scores[i]! >= bar) better.push({ ordinal, score: scores[i]! })
  })
  if (better.length === 0) return null
  return better
    .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score || a.ordinal - b.ordinal)
    .slice(0, LINK_CANDIDATES_MAX - 1)
    .map((b) => b.ordinal)
}

'''

The orchestrator asked for marked-session Stop to be cut before A and C. Measured on i1000 as a real git repo, interleaved against rc.4, the same written-back session:
- Before: +32.2 ms (+46.9%).
- After, repeated Stops: TS +2.3 ms (+3.4%), Rust core −15.2 ms (−22.7%).
- After, the first Stop after a new write (cache miss each time): TS +32.4 ms, Rust +20.1 ms.
In that fixture a whole-tree git status takes 94 ms and the scoped one 20.6 ms, the spawn floor (`git --version` 20.2 ms at load 8). What remains is one git spawn per writing turn.
payload.chose: Stop's git question (D11, D23) is scoped and cached, and the gate stays on. (1) Scope: `git status … -- <pathspecs>`. The pathspecs are every positive guard glob and file mention of an in-force rule, as `:(glob)**/<tail>` because a guard matches by tail. Any pattern git's glob cannot match as a guard does (`[`, `]`, `\`, `:`, a leading `/`, a `**` inside a segment) falls back to the whole tree. (2) Cache: the session's write mark counts may-write commands. Stop keeps git's answer under that count and a key of the pathspec set, and asks again only after another may-write command or a change in the rules' scope. A git failure is never cached.

payload.title: Runner test hygiene, found 2026-10-05. The pause/resume and fake-agent e2e tests leave their round.sh/run.ts children running when they time out: three fake-hold, fake-kill and fake-killbuild rounds outlived their test by 30 min, polling scratch dirs. Under load (one suite took 1,442 s with 8 timeouts, against ~90 s and 135/135 on the same commit) the 60 s and 240 s caps trip. Fix: kill the process group in afterEach/finally, and scale or relax the timeouts. Test-only, so not a deviation from PRE-REGISTRATION-R4 (the runner code is unchanged).

payload.text: Root cause of the 2026-10-05 ~14:00 runner-suite failures (8 timeouts, then 5 on re-run): the Mac was on BATTERY (88%, discharging). The real runner's L22 host-power gate waits for AC before launching, so the fake-agent e2e tests (authpause, chainm, pause/resume ×3) hung to their 60/240 s caps. The code is unchanged and passed 135/135 twice on AC at ≥4e8f070. Added to 5.8: the e2e tests must stub the host-power gate (or skip with a clear message on battery) and kill their round.sh children on timeout. Operational: round 4 also waits on battery, so start it on AC.

payload.because: Operator 2026-10-05: "It is always better to score after each rep… If rep 1 is already failing we can try and fix it and then start rep 2." Per-rep scoring is a hold plus scoring (not a deviation, PRE-REGISTRATION-R4 §9), and it allows an early futility stop that saves allowance. A mid-round fix is the one part that cannot stay inside round 4.
payload.chose: Score round 4 after each rep. Hold files park r2 and r3 behind each previous rep; when a rep's three arms finish, run score-batch, check-rep and round4_claims.py on the reps so far, then release the next rep. No product change happens between reps: rc.5 stays the pin for all of round 4. After any rep the operator may stop round 4 early for futility, fix, and re-test in a new round on a new held-out chain. That is logged as a deviation before the stop. A futility stop cannot raise a false win, but changing the product mid-round would break rep comparability and the freeze (D30).
payload.over: Scoring only after rep 3 (results wait ~2 days), or fixing sofar between reps and continuing round 4 on a new build (mixed versions; the frozen claims would no longer mean anything)
